summary: Follow-up plan for Layer GN.2 (quadratic and hermitian local-global theory), extending the accepted base packet, whose 55 GN.2 nodes (integral quadratic and hermitian lattices, localization and completion descent, genus and proper spinor genus, invariant factors, Voight's atomic forms, quaternionic hermitian data and the signed hermitian theory of Kurinczuk–Skodlerack–Stevens) are cited by id and not re-planned. It plans what that pass left open. (1) Lattices over a Dedekind domain: pseudobases, invariant factors and the Steinitz class; completion at a finite place; Voight's local-global dictionary; the R-index and the discriminant ideal. (2) Quaternion orders (the order notion moved down from ClassicalArithmeticCompletion), reduced discriminants, the maximality criterion and the Hasse–Schilling–Eichler norm theorem. (3) Finite fields: classification of quadratic forms in all characteristics with the Arf invariant, and the three geometrically irreducible quadric-surface types. (4) Local classifiers and their consumers: the genus character χ_d of a binary form with its local factors and the exponent-two genus theory; genus-character compatibility with imported binary local normal forms; odd unimodular representation of units; eigenspaces of isometries, the Cayley discriminant, Zassenhaus's spinor norm formula, integral spinor norms of regular quadratic modules through GSpin and the Chenevier–Taïbi constraint on characteristic polynomials; regular rank-at-least-three unimodular spinor images at nondyadic or hyperbolic-split places, with the general nonsplit dyadic case recorded as a gap. (5) Hermitian forms: the trace form and Jacobson's theorem, local and global classification, Jacobowitz's diagonalization over unramified extensions, scale and norm ideals, unimodular classification, hermitian genera, and Lipnowski–Tsimerman's model rings, unit labels and Gram-orbit bijection with their local lattice lemmas. (6) The complete signed hermitian transfer theory: unitary groups, equivariant linear forms, Witt parity, the determinant and standard values of the transfer, and the Skodlerack–Stevens theorem that the transfer preserves the maximal Witt element. (7) Routed paper items: Li's trace-unimodular O_F-lattices with a self-contained existence proof, Charles's Λ_{2d} transport and explicit plane, Lieblich–Maulik–Snowden's discriminant and norm-selection lemmas, and untwisted signature splitting and the line-valued direct-summand consequence with its localization input recorded as a gap.

nodes.title: Pseudobases and invariant factors of lattices over a Dedekind domain
nodes.statement: Let R be a Dedekind domain with fraction field F, V an n-dimensional F-vector space and M ⊆ V an R-lattice (a finitely generated R-submodule spanning V; Mathlib's Submodule.IsLattice F M). (a) For every F-basis y_1,…,y_n of V there are x_1,…,x_n ∈ M and nonzero fractional ideals 𝔞_1,…,𝔞_n of R with M = 𝔞_1x_1 ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ 𝔞_nx_n and x_j ∈ Fy_1 + ⋯ + Fy_j for every j (a pseudobasis with coefficient ideals 𝔞_j). (b) For n ≥ 1, dropping the triangularity condition, one may take 𝔞_1 = ⋯ = 𝔞_{n−1} = R, so M ≅ R^{n−1} ⊕ 𝔞 as R-modules. (c) For two R-lattices M, N ⊆ V there is a common pseudobasis x_1,…,x_n with M = ⊕𝔞_ix_i and N = ⊕𝔟_ix_i such that the ideals 𝔡_i = 𝔟_i𝔞_i^{−1} satisfy 𝔡_1 | 𝔡_2 | ⋯ | 𝔡_n; these invariant factors of N relative to M are unique. In particular every R-lattice is a finitely generated projective R-module, free exactly when it has a pseudobasis with all coefficient ideals principal.
hypotheses: R a Dedekind domain (not a field), F = Frac R, V finite-dimensional over F; n = 0 allowed (empty pseudobasis).
Fractional ideals are nonzero R-submodules of F; Mathlib's FractionalIdeal R⁰ F.
proofSteps: (a) Induct on n, with the zero-dimensional case empty. Intersect M with the first n−1 coordinate spaces. The last-coordinate image is a nonzero fractional ideal, hence an invertible projective module; the coordinate map splits. Its section extends over F to multiplication by a vector x_n. Rescale x_n and its coefficient ideal inversely to arrange x_n ∈ M. Induct on the kernel.

(b) For n ≥ 1 use the coprime-ideal form of Steinitz’s lemma: replace a fractional ideal by an equivalent ideal coprime to the other, using ideal approximation/two-generation, and split 𝔞 ⊕ 𝔟 as R ⊕ 𝔞𝔟. Iterate n−1 times.

(c) Local Smith normal form determines ordered exponents at each height-one prime; all but finitely many vanish, so unique ideal factorization reconstructs the invariant ideals and proves uniqueness. Existence of a single global pseudobasis simultaneously realizing them is a separate assertion of Voight Theorem 9.3.9: local bases cannot simply be glued. Its global elementary-divisor proof is the recorded common-pseudobasis gap; subsequent index computations use only the proved local exponents.
acceptance: R = ℤ: every lattice is free and (a) is the Hermite normal form of a basis.
R = ℤ[√−5], M = 𝔭 = (2, 1+√−5) ⊂ ℚ(√−5): n = 1, the only coefficient ideal is 𝔭 itself (up to principal ideals) and M is not free.
Invariant factors of 2ℤ ⊕ 6ℤ relative to ℤ²: (2), (6).

nodes.title: The Steinitz class of a lattice
nodes.statement: For an R-lattice M in an n-dimensional F-space V over a Dedekind domain R with pseudobasis M = 𝔞_1x_1 ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ 𝔞_nx_n (lattice-pseudobasis), the Steinitz class of M is st(M) = [𝔞_1⋯𝔞_n] ∈ Cl(R) (Mathlib's ClassGroup R; st(M) = 1 for n = 0). It does not depend on the pseudobasis, depends only on the isomorphism class of M as an R-module, and together with n classifies finitely generated torsion-free R-modules: M ≅ R^{n−1} ⊕ 𝔞 with [𝔞] = st(M) for n ≥ 1.
hypotheses: R Dedekind, F = Frac R, M ⊆ V an R-lattice; the class group is that of R, not a narrow or ray class group.
proofSteps: Independence: two pseudobases differ by a matrix g ∈ GL_n(F) with g·(⊕𝔞_i) = ⊕𝔟_i; comparing the top exterior powers gives 𝔟_1⋯𝔟_n = det(g)·𝔞_1⋯𝔞_n, so the classes agree.
Classification: lattice-pseudobasis (b) gives M ≅ R^{n−1} ⊕ 𝔞; R^{n−1} ⊕ 𝔞 ≅ R^{n−1} ⊕ 𝔟 forces [𝔞] = [𝔟] by the top exterior power.
acceptance: Over a PID every lattice has trivial Steinitz class.
𝔭 = (2, 1+√−5) in ℤ[√−5] has nontrivial class and 𝔭 ⊕ 𝔭 has trivial class, so 𝔭 ⊕ 𝔭 ≅ R² although 𝔭 is not free.

nodes.title: Completion of a lattice at a finite place
nodes.statement: Let R be a Dedekind domain with fraction field F, v a height-one prime of R (Mathlib's IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum R), F_v = adicCompletion F v and R_v = adicCompletionIntegers F v, and V_v = F_v ⊗_F V. For an R-lattice L ⊆ V its completion L_v ⊆ V_v is the R_v-span of the image of L. It is a full R_v-lattice; the natural map R_v ⊗_R L → V_v is injective with image L_v; L_v depends only on the localization L_(v); and if q : V → F is a quadratic map with q(L) ⊆ R, then the base-changed form q_v (Tau Ceti QuadraticForm.atFinitePlace when F is a number field) satisfies q_v(L_v) ⊆ R_v. Completion is monotone, commutes with finite sums and intersections of lattices, and sends cL to cL_v.
hypotheses: R Dedekind, not a field; V finite-dimensional over F; v ranges over the height-one primes (the finite places).
No freeness of L is assumed; L_v is free because R_v is a DVR.
proofSteps: A torsion-free module over a Dedekind domain is flat, so R_v is flat over R. Tensor the injection L → V with R_v. Since every nonzero element of R becomes invertible in F_v and Frac(R_v)=F_v, R_v ⊗_R V identifies with F_v ⊗_F V; the injection has image the R_v-span of L.
The image is finitely generated over R_v and spans V_v, so it is a full lattice; it is the R_v-span of L by construction.
Since L_(v) = R_(v)L and R_(v) → R_v, the completion of L equals that of L_(v); combine with completed-lattice-descent (R_(v) a DVR) to get L_v ∩ V = L_(v).
Integrality: q_v(Σ a_ix_i) = Σ a_i²q(x_i) + Σ_{i<j} a_ia_j polar(x_i,x_j) with a_i ∈ R_v and q(x_i), polar(x_i,x_j) ∈ R.
acceptance: L = 2ℤ: L_2 = 2ℤ_2 while L_3 = ℤ_3.
For the nonfree 𝔭 = (2, 1+√−5) ⊂ ℚ(√−5), the completion at 𝔭 is the principal ideal π R_𝔭 of the local ring.

nodes.title: Local-global dictionary for lattices
nodes.statement: Let R be a Dedekind domain with fraction field F, V a finite-dimensional F-space and M ⊆ V an R-lattice. (a) The map N ↦ (N_(𝔭))_𝔭 is a bijection from R-lattices N ⊆ V to families (N^𝔭)_𝔭 of R_(𝔭)-lattices in V, indexed by the maximal ideals, with N^𝔭 = M_(𝔭) for all but finitely many 𝔭; the inverse is (N^𝔭) ↦ ⋂_𝔭 N^𝔭. (b) The same holds with the completions N_v ⊆ V_v (lattice-completion) in place of the localizations: N ↦ (N_v)_v is a bijection onto the families of full R_v-lattices that agree with M_v for all but finitely many v, with inverse (N^v) ↦ V ∩ ⋂_v N^v. (c) Inclusion, sum, intersection and the R-index are computed place by place.
hypotheses: R Dedekind; M is only a reference lattice, and any two lattices agree at all but finitely many places.
This is a statement about embedded lattices, not about isometry classes.
proofSteps: Every lattice N satisfies rM ⊆ N ⊆ r^{−1}M for some nonzero r ∈ R (Voight Lemma 9.3.5), and r lies in only finitely many primes, so N_(𝔭) = M_(𝔭) for almost all 𝔭.

Injectivity is lattice-intersection-localizations. For surjectivity let N = ⋂_𝔭 N^𝔭; choose r with rM_(𝔭) ⊆ N^𝔭 ⊆ r^{−1}M_(𝔭) at the finitely many exceptional primes, so rM ⊆ N ⊆ r^{−1}M and N is a lattice; compute N_(𝔮) = N^𝔮 at each 𝔮 by choosing an element of the ideal of denominators outside 𝔮 (Voight's argument with unique factorization).
(b) follows from (a) and completed-lattice-descent at each prime, through lattice-completion.
(c): lattice-inclusion-localizations, and lattice-index-ideal for the index.
acceptance: The family (2ℤ_(2), ℤ_(p) for p odd) comes from 2ℤ.
A family differing from ℤ_(p) at infinitely many p (for example p^{-1}ℤ_(p) at every p) comes from no lattice: the intersection is not finitely generated over ℤ.

nodes.title: The R-index of two lattices
nodes.statement: For R-lattices M, N in an n-dimensional F-space V over a noetherian domain R, the R-index [M : N]_R is the R-submodule of F generated by det δ for all δ ∈ End_F(V) with δ(M) ⊆ N. It is a nonzero R-submodule; [αM : N] = det(α)^{−1}[M : N] for α ∈ Aut_F(V); for free M and N it is generated by the determinant of a change of basis; it commutes with localization; for projective M, N it is an invertible fractional ideal, and when N ⊆ M one has [M : N]_R = R iff M = N. Over a Dedekind domain with N ⊆ M it is the product of the invariant factors of the torsion module M/N, and over ℤ it is generated by #(M/N).
hypotheses: R noetherian domain for the definition; Dedekind for the invariant-factor and multiplicativity statements.
N ⊆ M is not required for the definition; [M : N]_R may be a non-integral fractional ideal.
proofSteps: Nonzero: some nonzero r ∈ R has rM ⊆ N, so r^n ∈ [M : N].
Free case: every δ with δ(M) ⊆ N factors as δ = δ₀∘(δ₀^{−1}δ) with δ₀ the change of basis and δ₀^{−1}δ an R-endomorphism of M, whose determinant lies in R.
Localization: clear denominators of finitely many generators of M (Voight Lemma 9.6.7).
Dedekind case: compute locally with Smith normal form and reassemble by unique factorization; multiplicativity [M : P] = [M : N][N : P] holds locally because determinants multiply.
acceptance: [M : rM]_R = r^nR (Voight Example 9.6.5).
[ℤ² : ℤ ⊕ 2ℤ]_ℤ = 2ℤ.

sources.locator: Definition 9.6.1, Lemmas 9.6.3–9.6.4, Examples 9.6.5–9.6.6, Lemma 9.6.7, Proposition 9.6.8, Lemma 9.6.9, printed pp.143–144
sources.match: Defines the R-index by determinants of maps carrying one lattice into the other, shows its behaviour under automorphisms, its principal generator for free lattices, its compatibility with localization, its invertibility for projective lattices and its description by invariant factors over a Dedekind domain.

nodes.title: Discriminant ideal and unimodularity of a quadratic lattice
nodes.statement: Let R be a Dedekind domain, F = Frac R, (V, q) a nondegenerate quadratic space of dimension n over F with polar form b(x,y) = q(x+y) − q(x) − q(y), and L ⊆ V an R-lattice. The discriminant ideal 𝔡(L) is the R-submodule of F generated by det(b(x_i,x_j))_{i,j} for all x_1,…,x_n ∈ L, and L^♯ = {y ∈ V : b(y, L) ⊆ R} is its dual lattice (the base packet's hermitian-dual-lattice with trivial involution). Then 𝔡(L) = [L^♯ : L]_R whenever L ⊆ L^♯ (that is, b is R-valued on L), 𝔡(N) = [L : N]_R²·𝔡(L) for any two lattices N, L, and for a pseudobasis L = ⊕𝔞_ix_i one has 𝔡(L) = det(b(x_i,x_j))·(𝔞_1⋯𝔞_n)². L is unimodular when L^♯ = L, equivalently (for L ⊆ L^♯) 𝔡(L) = R. For a different R-valued pairing Tr∘b the same construction gives the trace dual used for trace-unimodular lattices.

nodes.title: The genus character of a binary quadratic form
nodes.statement: Let d be a fundamental discriminant, d′ a discriminant (d′ ≡ 0, 1 mod 4, possibly a square) and D = dd′. For an integral binary quadratic form Q = [a, b, c] (Q(x, y) = ax² + bxy + cy²) of discriminant b² − 4ac = D, possibly imprimitive; both definite signs are allowed when D < 0, put χ_d(Q) = 0 if gcd(a, b, c, d) > 1, and otherwise χ_d(Q) = χ_d(m) := (d/m), the Kronecker symbol, for any integer m ≠ 0 represented by Q with gcd(m, d) = 1. Here χ_d(m) is Tau Ceti's genus character TauCeti.Multiquadratic.genusCharFun s m for the factorization s of d into distinct prime discriminants, with at most one even factor. The value lies in {0, ±1}.
hypotheses: d fundamental (d = 1 allowed, giving the trivial character); Q integral with discriminant dd′.
The form carrier and proper equivalence are those of IntegralLattices Layer B (milestones B1–B2) for the binary lattice with polar Gram [[2a, b], [b, 2c]]; no second carrier is introduced.
D ≠ 0 and d′ = D/d is 0 or 1 modulo 4. Negative definite forms are admitted so that negation is an operation on the domain.
proofSteps: For each prime p dividing d choose one of (1,0), (0,1), (1,1) with Q-value nonzero modulo p; otherwise a,c,a+b+c would all vanish modulo p. Choose a single pair (x,y) meeting these choices by CRT. Its value is coprime to d. Perturb the pair by multiples of the product of those primes if necessary to make the value nonzero; a nonzero binary polynomial cannot vanish on the entire resulting integer grid.
Use binary-form-genus-character-invariance, with GKZ’s quotient-discriminant condition, to prove independence of the represented value.
acceptance: d = 5, d′ = −3, D = −15, Q = 2x² + xy + 2y²: Q represents 2, and (5/2) = −1, so χ_5(Q) = −1, while the principal form x² + xy + 4y² has χ_5 = 1.

nodes.title: Well-definedness and invariance of the binary genus character
nodes.statement: In the setting of binary-form-genus-character: (a) χ_d(Q) does not depend on the represented integer m coprime to d; (b) χ_d(Q ∘ g) = χ_d(Q) for every g ∈ GL₂(ℤ), in particular for proper (SL₂(ℤ)) equivalence; (c) χ_d(−Q) = sgn(d)·χ_d(Q); (d) if D = dd′ with d′ also fundamental then χ_d(Q) = χ_{d′}(Q) whenever both are nonzero and Q is primitive; (e) for p | d and Q with gcd(a, b, c, d) = 1, the p-part of χ_d(Q) is (a, d)_p if p ∤ a and (c, d)_p if p ∤ c (Hilbert symbols), so χ_d(Q) = ∏_p χ_{d,p}(Q) with the local characters of local-genus-character.
hypotheses: d fundamental (1 allowed), disc Q = dd′ ≠ 0, d′ ≡ 0 or 1 mod 4; both signs of a definite form are in the domain. In (d), both factors d,d′ are fundamental.
proofSteps: (a) Use GKZ I.2 Proposition 1 at level one. At an odd prime-discriminant factor of d, choose a represented unit leading coefficient after an integral change of coordinates, then complete the square; all represented units have the same quadratic-residue character. At 2, the quotient d′ being 0 or 1 modulo 4 is needed: GKZ’s residue calculation for the even prime-discriminant factors −4, 8, −8 gives the same character for every represented odd value. Multiply the prime-discriminant characters. The pinned norm-identity lemma only covers fundamental D and cannot replace this dyadic calculation for arbitrary dd′.

(b) A unimodular integral substitution Q ∘ g preserves the represented set and coefficient content. This is the congruence action on binary forms, rather than the determinant-twisted conjugation action on trace-zero matrices.
(c) Negation replaces each represented value m by −m; the Kronecker character at −1 is sgn(d).
(d) Use CRT to choose a represented m coprime to D. For fundamental D and primitive Q, the represented-value norm identity makes χ_D(m)=1, and multiplicativity gives χ_d(m)χ_d′(m)=1.

(e) The local computations in (a), with the Hilbert-symbol formulas for the Kronecker factors, give χ_{d,p}(Q). At p|d, one of a,c is a unit: for odd p, divisibility of D forces b divisible if a,c are; for p=2 the discriminant condition forces b even.
acceptance: Over D = −15 the two genera {[1,1,4]} and {[2,1,2]} have χ_{−3} = 1, −1 and χ_5 = 1, −1, with χ_{−3}χ_5 = χ_{−15} = 1 on both.

nodes.title: Local genus characters on trace-zero matrices
nodes.statement: Let Δ be a fundamental discriminant (1 allowed), p a prime, and V the trace-zero matrices with Q(λ)=det λ. Write λ=[[b/2,−a],[c,−b/2]], with a,b,c ∈ ℤ_p exactly when λ ∈ L′_p, and D=b²−4ac. If p∤Δ define χ_{Δ,p} as the characteristic function of L′_p, including zero and imprimitive matrices. If p|Δ it is zero unless λ∈L′_p, D∈Δℤ_p, gcd(a,b,c,Δ) is a unit, and, when p=2, D/Δ belongs to 4ℤ₂ ∪ (1+4ℤ₂). On that support define it by (n,Δ)_p for any represented unit n of [a,b,c]. It is well defined, takes values 0,±1, and at p|Δ equals (a,Δ)_p when a is a unit or (c,Δ)_p when c is a unit. For h∈GL₂(ℤ_p), χ_{Δ,p}(hλh⁻¹)=(det h,Δ)_pχ_{Δ,p}(λ). The product on V(𝔸_f) is defined since almost all factors are 1; on a global form with disc=Δd′≠0, d′≡0,1 mod4, it equals the binary genus character.
hypotheses: Δ fundamental; V = trace-zero 2×2 rational matrices with Q = det, of signature (1,2); L′ the dual of the integral trace-zero matrices.
proofSteps: At p|Δ, apply the local residue calculation of GKZ I.2 Proposition 1. For p=2 it uses precisely the local quotient-discriminant condition D/Δ∈4ℤ₂∪(1+4ℤ₂). Existence of a represented unit follows from the three values a,c,a+b+c; D∈Δℤ_p then guarantees a or c is a unit.

At p∤Δ the published definition is the characteristic function of L′_p, with no primitivity requirement. This also covers λ=0. For an adele, λ_p∈L′_p at almost all p, and only finitely many p divide Δ, so the product is finite.

For S=[[0,1],[−1,0]], one has (hλh⁻¹)S=(det h)⁻¹h(λS)hᵀ. The congruence preserves represented values and multiplies the resulting binary form by (det h)⁻¹; its Hilbert character equals that of det h. Unit-square multiplication preserves the added dyadic support.

nodes.title: Genus characters evaluated through imported binary local normal forms
nodes.statement: Let Q be a primitive integral positive definite binary form of fundamental discriminant D<0. Import the ℤ_p normal-form classification from IntegralLattices 3C and 3D (and the base packet’s dyadic atomic form), rather than constructing it here. At an odd p|D, write its imported diagonal form as ux²+(D/u)vy² with u,v∈ℤ_p^×; then the p-part of its genus character is χ_{p*}(Q)=(u/p), where p*=(-1)^((p−1)/2)p. This value is independent of the chosen normal-form isometry. At 2 use local-genus-character with its corrected support and the imported even binary constituents.
hypotheses: Q primitive, D<0 fundamental; Khayutin Lemma B.1 is used only in this definite setting. IntegralLattices owns the full odd and dyadic normal-form theorems.
proofSteps: Import the normal-form existence and classification from IntegralLattices 3C/3D. Khayutin Lemma B.1 and Remark B.2 identify the same odd-prime coordinates.

The diagonal coefficient u is a represented unit, so local-genus-character gives (u,p*)_p=(u/p). Two normal-form choices give the same value by represented-value independence. The dyadic factors are evaluated by local-genus-character, without re-planning the upstream classification.

For D=−4, Q=[1,0,1], the dyadic local character equals 1, whereas [1,0,2] is excluded by the support test.

nodes.title: Genus theory when the class group has exponent two
nodes.statement: Let D′ < 0 be a fundamental discriminant with s distinct prime divisors, K = ℚ(√D′) and Cl(O_{D′}) its class group (equal to the narrow class group). The genus characters χ_Δ, for the factorizations D′ = ΔΔ̃ into fundamental discriminants, are exactly the characters of Cl/Cl², and #(Cl/Cl²) = 2^{s−1}. Consequently, if Cl has exponent at most 2 then h(D′) = 2^{s−1}, every character of Cl is a genus character, and the Hilbert class field of K is K(√Δ_1, …, √Δ_{s−1}) for the prime discriminants Δ_i dividing D′ (all but one of them).
hypotheses: D′ < 0 fundamental. The binary-form side is binary-form-genus-character through IntegralLattices B2 (forms ↔ classes).
proofSteps: Import Tau Ceti’s principal genus theorem and twoRank_eq_ncard_ramifiedPrimes_sub_one to identify the genus quotient and its order 2^{s−1}. Use IntegralLattices B2 only to translate ideal classes to primitive proper form classes.

Exponent at most two means Cl²=1, hence h=2^{s−1} and every class-group character is a genus character. There are 2^{s−1} sign-selected factorizations, not s (BEY’s proof typo is also recorded as PAPER-BRUINIER-EHLEN-YANG-21/E4).

Import isGenusField_candidateGenusField and finrank_candidateGenusField_over_candidateGenusFieldBase_eq_two_pow_ncard_ramifiedPrimes at the packet pin. They already supply the multiquadratic genus field, its everywhere-unramified property and degree 2^{s−1}. ClassFieldTheory 13 supplies the Hilbert class field and class-group degree; the genus field is contained in it and equal degrees force equality. No genus-field construction is planned here.
acceptance: D′ = −84 = (−3)(−4)(−7) (s = 3): Cl ≅ (ℤ/2)², h = 4 = 2², and the Hilbert class field of K = ℚ(√−21) is K(√−3, √−7), of degree 4 over K.
D′ = −23: s = 1, Cl ≅ ℤ/3 has exponent 3 and the conclusion h = 2^0 fails, as it must.

nodes.title: Signed hermitian spaces, their determinant and unitary group
nodes.statement: An ε-hermitian space over F/F_o is a finite-dimensional F-vector space V with a nondegenerate sesquilinear form h, conjugate-linear in the first variable, with h(w, v) = ε·h(v, w)‾. Its Gram matrix J in a basis satisfies J̄ᵀ = εJ and changes to B̄ᵀJB; det(V) is the class of det J in F^×/N_F, where N_F = N_{F/F_o}(F^×) if F/F_o is quadratic and (F^×)² if F = F_o. The adjoint anti-involution a ↦ ā of End_F(V) is defined by h(av, w) = h(v, āw), and U(V, h) = {a ∈ Aut_F(V) : āa = 1} is the isometry group: a unitary group if F ≠ F_o, a symplectic group if F = F_o and ε = −1, a full orthogonal group if F = F_o and ε = 1. An isometry (V, h) ≅ (V′, h′) induces U(V, h) ≅ U(V′, h′), but not conversely: over a nonarchimedean local quadratic extension of odd residue characteristic, odd-dimensional hermitian spaces have two isometry classes with isomorphic unitary groups.
hypotheses: For the definitions, a field of characteristic ≠2 with an involution of order at most two, finite-dimensional V, ε=±1 and a nondegenerate ε-hermitian form, conjugate-linear first.

The carrier and determinant are imported from the base packet’s signed-hermitian-witt-comparison and signed-hermitian-determinant-comparison. This node supplies the adjoint and unitary-group API. The assertion of exactly two odd-rank unitary isometry classes requires a nonarchimedean local quadratic extension of odd residue characteristic.
proofSteps: The adjoint exists and is unique by finite-dimensional duality: v ↦ h(v, ·) is a bijective semilinear map V → V^*.
Determinant: det(B̄ᵀJB) = N(det B)·det J, so the class modulo N_F is well defined; it is multiplicative for orthogonal sums.
Remark 3.11: scaling h by a non-norm α ∈ F_o^× multiplies det by α^n, which for odd n changes the class, while U(V, αh) = U(V, h).
acceptance: The hyperbolic plane has Gram matrix [[0, 1], [ε, 0]] and determinant class −ε.
F = ℂ, F_o = ℝ (the convention also applies archimedeanly): h(x, y) = x̄y on ℂ is hermitian with h(i, i) = 1.

nodes.title: Norms from a quadratic local extension versus squares
nodes.statement: Let F/F_o be a quadratic extension of nonarchimedean local fields of odd residue characteristic. (i) −1 ∈ (F^×)² iff −1 ∈ N_{F/F_o}(F^×). (ii) If −1 ∈ (F^×)² then N_{F/F_o}(F^×) = (F^×)² ∩ F_o^×. (iii) N_{F/F_o}(O_F^×) = (O_F^×)² ∩ F_o^×.
hypotheses: Odd residue characteristic is used for Hensel's lemma (1 + 𝔭_{F_o} ⊆ (O_{F_o}^×)²) and for the residue-field computation.
proofSteps: (iii) Reduce modulo 1 + 𝔭_{F_o}, which consists of squares, to the residue fields: if F/F_o is unramified both sides are k_{F_o}^× (the norm of finite fields is surjective), and if ramified both sides are (k_{F_o}^×)².

(i), (ii) follow from the base packet's odd-local-quadratic-norms, N(F^×) = ((F^×)² ∩ F_o^even) ∪ (−(F^×)² ∩ F_o^odd): if −1 is a square the second set lies in (F^×)², and conversely if −1 is a norm it lies in one of the two sets, the first since val(−1) = 0.
acceptance: F_o = ℚ_3, F = ℚ_3(√−1): −1 is a square in F, and the norms are (F^×)² ∩ ℚ_3^× = {x : val(x) even}.
F_o = ℚ_3, F = ℚ_3(√3): −1 is not a square in F (F's residue field is 𝔽_3) and −1 is not a norm.

sources.locator: Lemma 3.1 (i)–(ii) and equation (3.3) with its proof, p.10 (arXiv:1611.02667v3)
sources.match: States the description of the norm group, derives (i)–(iii) from it, and proves the unit statement (3.3) by Hensel and the residue fields.

nodes.title: Galois-equivariant linear forms on a self-dual extension
nodes.statement: Let (E, β) be a self-dual extension of F/F_o: E = F[β] a field to which the involution of F extends with β̄ = −β, fixed field E_o, n = [E : F]. An F-linear form λ : E → F is Galois-equivariant if λ(x̄) = λ(x)‾. The standard form λ_β is given by λ_β(1) = 1 and λ_β(β^i) = 0 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n − 1; it is Galois-equivariant. Every nonzero F-linear form on E is x ↦ λ_β(γx) for a unique γ ∈ E^×, and it is Galois-equivariant iff γ ∈ E_o^×.
hypotheses: Nonarchimedean local fields of odd residue characteristic; F/F_o quadratic or F = F_o, with the Galois involution x ↦ x̄; ε = ±1; h is sesquilinear, conjugate-linear in the first and linear in the second variable, with h(w, v) = ε·h(v, w)‾ (Mathlib's convention and that of Kurinczuk–Skodlerack–Stevens §3.2).
E/F finite with an extending involution; for β = 0 the extension is E = F and λ_β = id.
proofSteps: The standard functional is nonzero because λ_β(1)=1. For x≠0 choose z with λ_β(z)≠0 and put y=x⁻¹z; then λ_β(xy)≠0. Thus x↦λ_β(x·) is injective and, by equal finite dimensions, an isomorphism E→Hom_F(E,F). This argument does not require a triangular Gram matrix.
Equivariance of λ_β follows on the power basis: conjugation sends β^i to (−β)^i, and the coefficients are conjugated.

For f_γ(x)=λ_β(γx), one has overline(f_γ(x))=λ_β(overline(γ) overline(x)), whereas f_γ(overline(x))=λ_β(γ overline(x)). Equality for all x is equivalent to λ_β((γ−overline(γ))y)=0 for all y, hence to γ=overline(γ) by nondegeneracy.
acceptance: E = F, β = 0: λ_β = id, γ ∈ F_o^×.
E = F(β) with β² = b ∈ F_o, β̄ = −β, n = 2: λ_β(x + yβ) = x.

nodes.title: Even and odd parts of a signed hermitian Witt group
nodes.statement: For a finite extension E/E_o of the type above (E = E_o or quadratic) and ε = ±1, W^ε_even(E/E_o) ⊆ W^ε(E/E_o) is the subgroup of Witt classes of even anisotropic dimension; dim_an mod 2 : W^ε(E/E_o) → ℤ/2 is a homomorphism, and if W^ε(E/E_o) is nontrivial its kernel W^ε_even has index 2 and W^ε_odd is the nonidentity coset. The maximal element (the class of maximal anisotropic dimension) is the unique class fixed by all symmetric twists besides 0.
hypotheses: Nonarchimedean local fields of odd residue characteristic; F/F_o quadratic or F = F_o, with the Galois involution x ↦ x̄; ε = ±1; h is sesquilinear, conjugate-linear in the first and linear in the second variable, with h(w, v) = ε·h(v, w)‾ (Mathlib's convention and that of Kurinczuk–Skodlerack–Stevens §3.2).
proofSteps: Anisotropic dimensions add modulo 2 under orthogonal sum because hyperbolic planes are even-dimensional, so dim_an mod 2 is a homomorphism on W^ε.
It is surjective whenever a one-dimensional anisotropic space exists, i.e. outside the symplectic case F = F_o, ε = −1 (where W^ε = 0).
Maximal element: Kurinczuk–Skodlerack–Stevens Remark 3.9 lists it; Skodlerack–Stevens observe that symmetric twists act transitively on classes of fixed odd anisotropic dimension.
acceptance: Unitary case: W^ε has order 4, W^ε_even = {0, maximal element}, W^ε_odd the two one-dimensional classes.
Orthogonal case F = F_o: order 16, W_even of order 8.

sources.locator: §3.4, Remark 3.9 and Proposition 3.12, pp.13–14; §3.5, the paragraph before Proposition 3.14, p.15 (arXiv:1611.02667v3)

nodes.title: Transfer preserves the maximal Witt element (Skodlerack–Stevens)
nodes.statement: Let E/F be a finite extension of nonarchimedean local fields of odd residue characteristic, ρ an involution of F with fixed field F_o (possibly trivial), ρ′ an involution of E extending it, ε = ±1, and λ : E → F a nonzero ρ′-ρ-equivariant F-linear map. Then the transfer Tr_λ : W^ε(E/E_o) → W^ε(F/F_o), ⟨h̃⟩ ↦ ⟨λ ∘ h̃⟩, sends the maximal element X_{ρ′,ε,E} to the maximal element X_{ρ,ε,F}. In addition Tr_λ is bijective when [E : F] is odd, and for ε = +1 and [E : F] = 2 with F = F_o its image has at least four elements, it is injective when E ≠ E_o, and its kernel has exactly four elements, all of anisotropic dimension at most 2, when E = E_o.
hypotheses: Nonarchimedean local fields of odd residue characteristic; F/F_o quadratic or F = F_o, with the Galois involution x ↦ x̄; ε = ±1; h is sesquilinear, conjugate-linear in the first and linear in the second variable, with h(w, v) = ε·h(v, w)‾ (Mathlib's convention and that of Kurinczuk–Skodlerack–Stevens §3.2).
This is the input cited as [39, Theorem 4.4] in Kurinczuk–Skodlerack–Stevens Proposition 3.13(ii).
proofSteps: First handle the symplectic case of trivial involutions and ε=−1: both Witt groups are zero and the maximal element is zero. When the involution is nontrivial, a skew scalar identifies the two signs and commutes with transfer. Change of an equivariant functional is a symmetric twist (equivariant-linear-form).

The image of the maximal element is fixed by all symmetric twists by elements of F_o^× (they commute with Tr_λ), hence is 0 or the maximal element (signed-witt-parity); it suffices to show it is nonzero.
Odd degree: Tr_λ⟨1⟩ has odd anisotropic dimension and its twists generate, so Tr_λ is surjective, hence bijective by counting (Proposition 4.6).

Transitivity in towers reduces to quadratic E/F; with λ = Tr_{E/F} compute Gram matrices in the basis 1, α (α a skew-symmetric uniformizer) and choose δ with −det not a square to get a nonzero image (Lemma 4.7); conclude in the remaining quadratic cases.
acceptance: Skodlerack–Stevens Example 4.3: E = ℚ_3(√3, √5), F = ℚ_3(√5), ρ′(√5) = −√5: the transfer kills ⟨√3⟩ but sends ⟨√3⟩ ⊕ ⟨1⟩ (maximal) to the maximal class.

sources.locator: §4: Theorem 4.1, Definitions 4.2 and 4.5, Example 4.3, Theorem 4.4, Proposition 4.6, Lemma 4.7 and the proof of Theorem 4.4, pp.8–11 (arXiv:1503.08882v3)
sources.match: Theorem 4.4 states that the transfer of the maximal anisotropic class of E is the maximal anisotropic class of F; Proposition 4.6 proves bijectivity in odd degree and Lemma 4.7 the quadratic case with the kernel description; the proof combines them through symmetric twists and transitivity in towers.

nodes.title: Determinant of a transferred signed hermitian space
nodes.statement: Let (E, β) be a self-dual extension of F/F_o, n = [E : F], and λ a nonzero Galois-equivariant F-linear form on E. For every ε-hermitian space (V, h) over E/E_o, det(λ_*V) = det(λ_*⟨1⟩_{+})^{dim_E V}·N_{E/F}(det V) in F^×/N_F. The auxiliary line ⟨1⟩_{+} always has sign +1, regardless of the sign of V. For F = F_o and ε = 1 (quadratic forms, trivial involution) this is Scharlau's determinant formula for the transfer s_*(q).
hypotheses: Nonarchimedean local fields of odd residue characteristic; F/F_o quadratic or F = F_o, with the Galois involution x ↦ x̄; ε = ±1; h is sesquilinear, conjugate-linear in the first and linear in the second variable, with h(w, v) = ε·h(v, w)‾ (Mathlib's convention and that of Kurinczuk–Skodlerack–Stevens §3.2).
proofSteps: Choose an F-basis of E and an E-basis of V. Let C be the Gram matrix of (x,y)↦λ(overline(x)y), namely the transferred +1 line. The matrix of the transferred form is a block matrix with baseline determinant (det C)^m and an E-linear Gram change of determinant det_E J. Its F-determinant is N_{E/F}(det_E J), yielding (det C)^mN(det J). This uses restriction-of-scalars determinants and works for alternating forms too.

A change of E-basis multiplies det J by a norm, and the corresponding F-basis change multiplies the transferred determinant by a square/norm. Thus the identity descends to F^×/N_F. No one-dimensional alternating line is introduced.
acceptance: n = 1 (E = F, λ = id): det(V) = det(V).
V hyperbolic over E: λ_*V = nH has det (−ε)^n, and det(λ_*⟨1⟩)²·N(−ε) gives the same class.

sources.locator: Proposition 3.15(i) and the first sentence of its proof, pp.15–16 (arXiv:1611.02667v3)
sources.match: States the determinant of the transfer as det(λ_*⟨1⟩)^{dim V} times the norm of det V and refers to Scharlau, Lemma 5.8, for the quadratic-form analogue, the hermitian case following with extra signs.

nodes.title: The standard transfer of ⟨1⟩ and ⟨β⟩
nodes.statement: Let (E, β) be a self-dual extension of F/F_o with n = [E : F] and λ_β the standard form. In W^1(F/F_o): λ_{β*}⟨1⟩ ≅ ((n−1)/2)H ⊕ ⟨1⟩ if n is odd and ≅ ((n−2)/2)H ⊕ ⟨1⟩ ⊕ ⟨(−1)^{n/2+1}N_{E/F}(β)⟩ if n is even. In W^{−1}(F/F_o): λ_{β*}⟨β⟩ = ⟨(−1)^{(n−1)/2}N_{E/F}(β)⟩ if n is odd and 0 if n is even. Consequently, when F/F_o is quadratic, λ_{β*} is determined on all of W^ε(E/E_o) by these values, signed-transfer-determinant and the classification by dimension and determinant.
hypotheses: Nonarchimedean local fields of odd residue characteristic; F/F_o quadratic or F = F_o, with the Galois involution x ↦ x̄; ε = ±1; h is sesquilinear, conjugate-linear in the first and linear in the second variable, with h(w, v) = ε·h(v, w)‾ (Mathlib's convention and that of Kurinczuk–Skodlerack–Stevens §3.2).
The ⟨β⟩ statement requires β≠0. For β=0 one has E=F and only the +1 line ⟨1⟩ and identity transfer are asserted.
proofSteps: Let X^n + b_{n−1}X^{n−1} + ⋯ + b_0 be the minimal polynomial of β. In the basis 1, β, …, β^{n−1} the Gram matrix of λ_{β*}⟨1⟩ has entries (−1)^i λ_β(β^{i+j}), which vanish for 1 ≤ i + j ≤ n − 1; its first row and column are (1, 0, …, 0), and the anti-diagonal below is ±b_0.
For n odd, the span of β, …, β^{n−1} has the totally isotropic subspace spanned by β, …, β^{(n−1)/2} of half its dimension, so it is hyperbolic.
For n even, split off ⟨1⟩ and a hyperbolic part of dimension n − 2, and read the remaining one-dimensional class from the determinant (signed-transfer-determinant), N_{E/F}(β) = (−1)^n b_0.
The ⟨β⟩ case is the same computation for the skew-hermitian form, or follows from (i) and a twist by β.
Unitary case: an ε-hermitian space over a quadratic F/F_o is determined by dimension and determinant (Kurinczuk–Skodlerack–Stevens Remark 3.10).
acceptance: n = 2, β² = b: λ_{β*}⟨1⟩ = ⟨1⟩ ⊕ ⟨N_{E/F}(β)⟩ = ⟨1⟩ ⊕ ⟨−b⟩, matching the Gram matrix diag(1, −b) of x + yβ ↦ λ_β((x+yβ)‾(x+yβ)).

sources.match: Gives the transfer of ⟨1⟩ and ⟨β⟩ under λ_β in both parities, with the Gram matrix in the power basis and the hyperbolic splitting, and remarks that in the unitary case these values determine the standard transfer completely.

nodes.title: The trace quadratic form of a hermitian space
nodes.statement: Let E/F be a quadratic extension of fields of characteristic ≠ 2 with conjugation x ↦ x̄, and (V, h) a hermitian space over E (conjugate-linear in the first variable, h(w, v) = h(v, w)‾). Its trace form is the F-quadratic space (V_F, q_h) with q_h(v) = h(v, v) ∈ F and polar form Tr_{E/F}h(v, w) = h(v, w) + h(w, v), whose diagonal is 2q_h. If h ≅ ⟨a_1, …, a_n⟩ (a_i ∈ F^×) and E = F(√δ), then q_h ≅ ⟨a_1, …, a_n⟩ ⊗ ⟨1, −δ⟩. Jacobson's theorem: two hermitian spaces over E are isometric iff their trace forms are isometric over F. Zhang's convention, linear in the first variable, is h′(v, w) = h(w, v); it has the same trace form.
hypotheses: char F ≠ 2; E/F a separable quadratic field extension (the split algebra E = F × F is excluded here).
proofSteps: q_h is quadratic: q_h(cv) = N(c)q_h(v) and its polar form is Tr∘h, F-bilinear and symmetric.
A hermitian space has an orthogonal basis (char ≠ 2), and q_{⟨a⟩}(x) = a·N_{E/F}(x) = a(x_1² − δx_2²).

Jacobson: choose a nonzero-norm vector e in h′ (an orthogonal basis exists). A trace-form isometry shows that q_h represents c=h′(e,e), so split the hermitian line ⟨c⟩ from h and h′. Their trace forms split the common regular binary norm form cN_{E/F}; quadratic Witt cancellation gives isometric trace forms of the complements. Induct on the E-dimension; dimension zero is immediate. Conversely a hermitian isometry preserves the trace form.
acceptance: E = ℂ, F = ℝ, h = ⟨1⟩: q_h = x² + y², positive definite of rank 2.
h = ⟨1⟩ ⊕ ⟨−1⟩ (hyperbolic) has hyperbolic trace form of rank 4.

nodes.title: Classification of hermitian spaces over local and global fields
nodes.statement: Let E/F be a quadratic extension. (a) If F is a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic 0, hermitian spaces over E are classified by dimension and determinant in F^×/N_{E/F}(E^×); each class (n, d) occurs for n ≥ 1. (b) If F is a number field, hermitian spaces over E are classified by dimension, determinant in F^×/N(E^×) and the signatures at the real places of F that do not split in E; equivalently, two hermitian spaces are isometric iff they are isometric at every place (Landherr's Hasse principle).
hypotheses: Characteristic 0; E a field.
proofSteps: (a) By hermitian-trace-form, h ↦ q_h is injective on isometry classes; q_{⟨a_1,…,a_n⟩} = ⟨a_i⟩ ⊗ N_{E/F} has dimension 2n, discriminant δ^n and Hasse invariant determined by ∏a_i mod norms (the Hilbert symbol (∏a_i, δ)); apply the local classification (QuadraticFormInvariants 6D).

(b) Local isometry everywhere gives local isometry of the trace forms everywhere, hence a global isometry of q_h (GlobalQuadraticForms Layer 6), hence of h; the invariants (dim, det, signatures) determine all local classes by (a) and by Sylvester at real places.
acceptance: Over ℚ_p with E unramified: ⟨1⟩ and ⟨p⟩ are the two hermitian lines.
For ℂ/ℝ, ⟨1,1⟩ and ⟨−1,−1⟩ have determinant 1 modulo norms but signatures (2,0) and (0,2), hence are not isometric. N(i)=1, so i cannot turn a positive line into a negative line.

nodes.title: Hermitian lattices over an unramified extension have orthogonal bases
nodes.statement: Let E/F be an unramified quadratic extension of nonarchimedean local fields (any residue characteristic) with uniformizer ϖ ∈ F, and L a nondegenerate hermitian O_E-lattice of rank n. Then L has an orthogonal O_E-basis with Gram matrix diag(ϖ^{λ_1}, …, ϖ^{λ_n}), λ_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ λ_n, and the tuple λ is unique: it is the tuple of base packet hermitian-lattice-invariants (after reordering and shifting by the scale). Equivalently, the space X_n of nondegenerate hermitian matrices in GL_n(E) decomposes as ⊔_{λ ∈ P_n} GL_n(O_E)·ϖ^λ under X ↦ gXḡᵀ, with P_n the nonincreasing integer tuples; the subset whose entries lie in O_E corresponds to λ_n ≥ 0. This integral-entry subset is not the scheme-theoretic GL_n(O_E) condition, which would require unit determinant.
hypotheses: E/F unramified, so Tr_{E/F} : O_E → O_F and N_{E/F} : O_E^× → O_F^× are surjective (also when the residue characteristic is 2).
proofSteps: Unramifiedness makes the residue extension separable quadratic; its trace is onto the residue field. Reduction of the integral trace and Nakayama show Tr(O_E)=O_F, and one can choose a unit with unit trace. If a diagonal pairing already realizes the minimal scale valuation m, split it. Otherwise choose x,y with h(x,y)=ϖ^m u and both diagonal entries of strictly larger valuation. Choose a unit t with Tr(overline(t)u) a unit; the cross term makes h(x+ty,x+ty) have valuation m, including residue characteristic two. The resulting Gram entry divides all pairings, so this rank-one summand splits integrally.
Normalize the diagonal unit to 1 using surjectivity of the norm on units; induct on the rank.
Uniqueness: L^∨/L ≅ ⊕ O_E/ϖ^{λ_i} after scaling, so λ is determined by the invariant factors (base packet dvr-ordered-exponent-uniqueness).
acceptance: n = 1: the lattice O_E e with h(e, e) = ϖ³u is equivalent to ϖ³ (λ = (3)).
The hermitian matrix [[0, 1], [1, 0]] is GL₂(O_E)-equivalent to diag(1, −1) ~ diag(1, 1): λ = (0, 0).

nodes.title: Local classification of unimodular hermitian lattices
nodes.statement: Let E/F be a quadratic extension of nonarchimedean local fields and V a nondegenerate hermitian space over E. If E/F is unramified, or ramified with odd residue characteristic, then any two unimodular hermitian O_E-lattices in V are isometric under U(V). In the ramified dyadic case the same holds for unimodular lattices with equal norm ideals.
hypotheses: Unimodular means L^∨ = L for h (base packet hermitian-dual-lattice).
proofSteps: Unramified: unramified-hermitian-lattice-diagonalization with λ = 0 gives an orthonormal basis, so all unimodular lattices are isometric to O_E^n with the standard form.

Ramified, odd residue characteristic: Tr(O_E) = O_F since 2 is a unit, so the splitting argument above gives an orthogonal basis with unit diagonal u_i ∈ O_F^×; binary ⟨u, u′⟩ ≅ ⟨1, uu′⟩ by the norm/trace argument, so the lattice is ⟨1, …, 1, det⟩; det mod N(O_E^×) = (O_F^×)² (quadratic-norm-squares (iii)) is determined by det V because N(E^×) ∩ O_F^× = N(O_E^×). Both lattices are thus isometric, and an isometry of lattices extends to an element of U(V).
Ramified dyadic: the input is Jacobowitz, Proposition 10.4; recorded as a gap.
acceptance: E/F unramified: O_E^n is the unique unimodular lattice up to isometry in its space.
Ramified odd: the lattices ⟨1, 1⟩ and ⟨1, u⟩ (u a nonsquare unit) live in spaces of different determinant.

nodes.title: Scale and norm ideals of a local hermitian lattice
nodes.statement: For a hermitian O_E-lattice L in a hermitian space over a quadratic extension E/F of local fields, the scale 𝔰(L) ⊆ E is the O_E-submodule generated by the values h(x, y), x, y ∈ L, and the norm ideal 𝔫(L) ⊆ F is the O_F-submodule generated by the values h(x, x), x ∈ L. Both are isometry invariants with Tr(𝔰(L)) ⊆ 𝔫(L) ⊆ 𝔰(L) ∩ F, and for E/F unramified or of odd residue characteristic 𝔫(L) = 𝔰(L) ∩ F.
hypotheses: E/F quadratic, local; L full O_E-lattice; F-valued norm ideal (Lipnowski–Tsimerman write it as an O_{L_v}-ideal; here the O_F-module is primary and O_E·𝔫(L) is its extension).
proofSteps: Invariance under isometry is immediate from the definitions.
Tr(h(x, y)) = h(x + y, x + y) − h(x, x) − h(y, y) gives Tr(𝔰) ⊆ 𝔫; if the trace O_E → O_F is surjective (unramified or odd), Tr(𝔰) = 𝔰 ∩ F.

Lipnowski–Tsimerman generate their norm ideal over O_E. Its relation to this O_F-valued convention is extension of ideals: 𝔫_LT(L)=𝔫(L)O_E. State this adapter explicitly before using determinant/norm-ideal labels from that paper.
acceptance: L = O_E with h = ⟨1⟩: 𝔰 = O_E, 𝔫 = O_F.
Ramified dyadic E = ℚ_2(i): the lattice O_E² with the hyperbolic Gram [[0, 1], [1, 0]] has 𝔫 = Tr(O_E) = 2ℤ_2 ≠ 𝔰 ∩ F = ℤ_2.

nodes.title: Genus and class set of hermitian lattices over a number field
nodes.statement: Let L/K be a quadratic extension of number fields (for Lipnowski–Tsimerman a CM field over its totally real subfield) and (V, h) a hermitian space. Two O_L-lattices M, M′ ⊆ V are in the same genus if M_v ≅ M′_v under U(V)(K_v) at every finite place v of K; the classes in the genus of M are the U(V)(K)-orbits of lattices in it. The class set is in bijection with U(V)(K)\U(V)(𝔸_K^f)/Stab(M̂), by the lattice local-global dictionary.
hypotheses: Lattices are projective O_L-modules of full rank (not necessarily free); U(V) is the unitary group of signed-hermitian-space over K.
proofSteps: The adelic group acts on lattices through completions (lattice-completion) and the local-global dictionary (lattice-local-global-dictionary); the orbit of M is its genus and the stabilizer is the product of the local stabilizers.
acceptance: For L = ℚ(i), K = ℚ, V = L² with the standard form: M = O·(1, 1)/(1+i) ⊕ O·(1, −1)/(1+i) is unimodular with an orthonormal basis, differs from O², and lies in the genus (indeed the class) of O².

nodes.title: Unit-norm labels and the hermitian forms ⟨·,·⟩_σ
nodes.statement: Let L be a CM field with totally real subfield K, Σ = O_K^{×,+}/N_{L/K}(O_L^×) the finite group of totally positive units modulo norms of units, and ε_σ a chosen representative of σ ∈ Σ (ε_1 = 1). For n≥1, on L^n put ⟨z, w⟩_σ = ε_σ z_1 w̄_1 + Σ_{i≥2} z_i w̄_i (Lipnowski–Tsimerman's convention, linear in the first variable). It is a totally positive definite hermitian form with determinant ε_σ, and the free unimodular O_L-lattices of determinant class σ lie in the space of ⟨·,·⟩_σ.
hypotheses: L CM over K; Σ is finite because N(O_L^×) ⊇ (O_K^×)² (Dirichlet's unit theorem gives [O_K^{×}: (O_K^×)²] finite).
The labelled n-dimensional form requires n≥1; the zero-dimensional form has no nontrivial determinant label.
proofSteps: Σ is a quotient of O_K^{×,+}/(O_K^×)², which is a finite elementary abelian 2-group.
⟨·,·⟩_σ is positive definite at every real place since ε_σ is totally positive; its Gram matrix diag(ε_σ, 1, …, 1) has determinant ε_σ.
acceptance: L = ℚ(i): K = ℚ, O_K^{×,+} = {1}, Σ trivial.
L = ℚ(√2, i): O_K^{×,+} is generated by (1+√2)² up to sign, and that is N(1+√2), so Σ is trivial too.

nodes.title: Positive hermitian unimodular matrices and free unimodular lattices
nodes.statement: Let L be a CM field with totally real subfield K and GL_n(O_L)^+ the totally positive definite hermitian matrices in GL_n(O_L). The orbits of GL_n(O_L) on GL_n(O_L)^+ under A ↦ g*Ag correspond bijectively to ⊔_{σ ∈ Σ} {free unimodular O_L-lattices in (L^n, ⟨·,·⟩_σ) of determinant class σ}/U_σ(K), a lattice going to its Gram matrix in any basis. Every class of free unimodular lattices of a given (σ, norm ideal) lies in one genus.
hypotheses: Positive definiteness at every real place; free lattices only (projective ones are counted by free-projective-hermitian-comparison).
proofSteps: Given A, the form ⟨Az, w⟩ has determinant det A ∈ O_K^{×,+}, whose class σ_A ∈ Σ is constant on orbits; by hermitian-space-classification it is isometric to ⟨·,·⟩_{σ_A} (same determinant modulo norms, same signatures), and an isometry φ_A carries O_L^n to a free unimodular lattice; independence of φ_A modulo U_σ.
Inverse: Gram matrix of a basis of a free unimodular lattice; a change of basis acts by *-conjugation.
acceptance: n = 1: orbits of O_L^× on O_K^{×,+} by u ↦ N(g)u are exactly Σ.
L = ℚ(i), n = 2: [[2, 1], [1, 1]] = ḡᵀg for g = [[1, 0], [1, 1]], so it lies in the orbit of I_2.

sources.match: Proves the bijection between *-conjugation orbits of positive unimodular hermitian matrices and free unimodular lattices of each determinant label, through the local classification and the hermitian Hasse principle, and refines it by norm ideals into single genera.

nodes.title: Free versus projective unimodular hermitian lattices
nodes.statement: Fix a labelled positive hermitian space V_σ and a local norm-ideal profile as in free-unimodular-gram-orbits. The classes of free unimodular O_L-lattices in this fixed space and profile form a subset of the classes of projective unimodular lattices there. A projective lattice is free exactly when its Steinitz class is trivial; consequently the subsets agree when Cl(O_L)=1. For a general projective lattice, there is no chosen global basis or canonical unit Gram determinant: one first fixes the rational hermitian space and then uses its determinant class and local norm ideals.
hypotheses: The rank n is positive; the hermitian space and norm-ideal profile are fixed before making the comparison. Class number one is sufficient, not necessary.
proofSteps: Free lattices are projective. A projective lattice is free iff its Steinitz class is trivial (lattice-steinitz-class), which is automatic when Cl(O_L) = 1.
acceptance: L = ℚ(i): Cl = 1, so every unimodular O_L-lattice is free.
L = ℚ(√−5): the rank-one lattice 𝔭 = (2, 1+√−5) with h = ⟨1/2⟩·N is projective, unimodular for a suitable scaling, and not free.

sources.match: Notes that the mass-formula side counts projective hermitian lattices, not only free ones, so the free count is bounded by it.

nodes.title: Model rings with positive involution
nodes.statement: A model ring with positive involution is R_{L,n} = ∏_{i=1}^k M_{n_i}(O_{L_i}) with (M_1, …, M_k)* = (M̄_1ᵀ, …, M̄_kᵀ), for a finite indexed family of CM fields L_i (repetitions allowed) with totally real subfields K_i and positive integers n_i with Σ_i n_i[L_i : ℚ] = 2g. Its quaternionic analogue is M_m(O_D) for a maximal order O_D of a totally definite quaternion algebra D over a totally real field, with (M)* = M̄ᵀ for the canonical involution. The positive symmetric units are R^{×,+} = {a ∈ R^× : a* = a, a totally positive definite}, on which R^× acts by g·a = g*ag; the orbit count n_{L,n} is the number of orbits.
hypotheses: Indexed by the simple factors: two factors with isomorphic L_i keep separate central idempotents.
proofSteps: The orbit set factors as the product over i of the orbit sets of GL_{n_i}(O_{L_i}) on GL_{n_i}(O_{L_i})^+, each described by free-unimodular-gram-orbits.
acceptance: k = 1, L = ℚ(i), n = 1: R = ℤ[i] with complex conjugation; R^{×,+} = {1}, one orbit.
Repetition: two factors ℚ(i) give R = ℤ[i] × ℤ[i], with orbit set the product.

nodes.title: Local monogenic orders and their lattices
nodes.statement: Let f ∈ ℤ_ℓ[x] be monic irreducible with separable root field F = ℚ_ℓ[x]/(f), R = ℤ_ℓ[x]/(f) ⊆ O_F the monogenic order and δ = v_ℓ(disc f). An R-lattice of rank n is a full ℤ_ℓ-lattice in F^n stable under R. Its O_F-saturation is O_F·M. By Euler's lemma the trace dual of R is f′(θ)^{−1}R, so R ⊆ O_F ⊆ R^∨ = f′(θ)^{−1}R and [R^∨ : R] = ℓ^δ; the conductor 𝔣 = {x : xO_F ⊆ R} satisfies 𝔣·𝔡_{O_F} = f′(θ)O_F.
hypotheses: ℓ prime; F a field (f irreducible); R need not be Dedekind and R-lattices need not be free.
For the different/conductor identity, O_F is the integral closure of ℤ_ℓ in F and F/ℚ_ℓ is finite separable; f is the monic minimal polynomial of the integral generator θ.
proofSteps: Euler's lemma is Mathlib's traceForm_dualSubmodule_adjoin; the conductor-different identity is conductor_mul_differentIdeal; disc f = ±N(f′(θ)).
acceptance: f = x² + 1 over ℤ_3: R = O_F, δ = 0.
f = x² + 4 over ℤ_2: R = ℤ_2[2i] has index 2 in O_F = ℤ_2[i], and δ = v_2(−16) = 4.

nodes.title: Normalized orbit representatives of R-lattices
nodes.statement: In the setting of local-monogenic-order, every R-lattice M ⊆ F^n is GL_n(F)-equivalent to a lattice M′ with R^n ⊆ M′ ⊆ O_F^n; then #(M′/R^n) ≤ #(O_F/R)^n ≤ ℓ^{δn}. If moreover γ-stable lattices for a semisimple γ with characteristic polynomial f^n are identified with R-lattices, the GL_n(F)-orbits of γ-stable lattices are represented by sublattices of colength at most δn in O_F^n.
hypotheses: F a field; GL_n(F) acts on F^n; O_F^n is the unique saturated lattice up to GL_n(F).
proofSteps: GL_n(F) acts transitively on O_F-lattices, so move O_F·M to O_F^n. Choose m_i ∈ M forming an O_F-basis of O_F^n (Nakayama on M → O_F^n/𝔪O_F^n), write m_i = Ae_i with A ∈ GL_n(O_F) and replace M by A^{−1}M ⊇ R^n.
O_F^n/R^n injects into (R^∨/R)^n, of size ℓ^{δn}.
acceptance: n = 1: every R-lattice M ⊆ F is F^×-equivalent to an R-module M′ with R ⊆ M′ ⊆ O_F, for example R or O_F itself.

nodes.title: Stable lattices with prescribed flag quotients
nodes.statement: Let γ be a semisimple endomorphism of a finite-dimensional ℚ_ℓ-space V with a γ-stable subspace V_1, π : V → V/V_1, and fix γ-stable lattices U_1 ⊆ V_1 and U_2 ⊆ V/V_1. For a γ-equivariant projection p : V → V_1, the assignment L ↦ φ_L (u ↦ p(any lift of u to L) mod U_1) is a well-defined map from γ-stable lattices L with L ∩ V_1 = U_1 and π(L) = U_2 to Hom_{ℤ_ℓ[γ]}(U_2, V_1/U_1)/Hom_{ℤ_ℓ[γ]}(U_2, V_1), independent of p; its fibres lie in single orbits of the subgroup of the centralizer of γ acting identically on V₁ and V/V₁.
hypotheses: γ semisimple, so γ-equivariant projections onto V_1 exist.
proofSteps: Two lifts of u differ by an element of L ∩ V_1 = U_1; two projections differ by a ℤ_ℓ[γ]-map U_2 → V_1, which is quotiented out.

If φ_{L_1} = φ_{L_2}, write V = V_1 ⊕ ker p_2 = V_1 ⊕ ker p_1; the map that is the identity on V_1 and sends b ∈ ker p_2 to T(πb) + (π|ker p_1)^{−1}(πb) commutes with γ, is unipotent, and carries L_2 to L_1 (Lipnowski–Tsimerman Lemma 3.1).
acceptance: V_1 = V: the fibre is a single lattice.
γ = identity on ℚ_ℓ², V_1 = ℚ_ℓe_1, U_i = ℤ_ℓ: the lattices are ℤ_ℓ(e_2 + te_1) + ℤ_ℓe_1 with t ∈ ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ, all in one unipotent orbit.

nodes.title: Index of a lattice under a stable endomorphism
nodes.statement: Let O be a DVR with finite residue field of size q, valuation v, fraction field K, and T a free O-lattice spanning a finite-dimensional K-space W. If F ∈ GL_K(W) and F(T) ⊆ T, then T/F(T) and F^{−1}(T)/T are finite of cardinality q^{v(det F)}, and F induces an O-linear isomorphism F^{−1}(T)/T ≅ T/F(T). This includes rank 0 and v(det F) = 0.
hypotheses: Finite residue field; F invertible on W.
proofSteps: The index ideal [T : F(T)]_O is (det F) (lattice-index-ideal, free case); over a DVR its cardinality is q^{v(det F)} (Smith normal form).
F restricts to an isomorphism F^{−1}(T) → T carrying T onto F(T).
acceptance: W = K, F = multiplication by π^k: #(T/FT) = q^k.
F = id: both quotients are 0.

nodes.title: Isotypic stabilizers contain a congruence kernel
nodes.statement: In the setting of local-monogenic-order with S = O_F and β = f′(θ): if R^n ⊆ M ⊆ S^n then ker(GL_n(S) → GL_n(S/βS)) ⊆ Stab(M), hence [GL_n(S) : Stab_{GL_n(S)}(M)] ≤ #M_n(S/βS) = ℓ^{n²δ_S} with ℓ^{δ_S} = #(S/βS), and this includes δ_S = 0 where the stabilizer is GL_n(S).
hypotheses: This is the isotypic case only; the nonisotypic global exponent of Lipnowski–Tsimerman (20) is a separate (Layer 3) target.
proofSteps: βS ⊆ R by conductor_mul_differentIdeal (β ∈ 𝔣·𝔡 ⊆ 𝔣), so βS^n ⊆ R^n ⊆ M. For g ≡ 1 mod β: (g − 1)M ⊆ βS^n ⊆ M, so gM ⊆ M; apply to g^{−1}.
The index of a subgroup containing the kernel is at most the size of the image in GL_n(S/βS) ⊆ M_n(S/βS).
acceptance: δ_S = 0 (R = S, β a unit): Stab(M) = GL_n(S) and the bound is 1.

nodes.title: Unique local orbit of stable lattices at good primes
nodes.statement: Let γ be semisimple on a finite-dimensional ℚ_ℓ-space V with monic squarefree minimal polynomial f ∈ ℤ_ℓ[T] of unit discriminant. Then R = ℤ_ℓ[γ] is finite étale over ℤ_ℓ and equal to its maximal order S = ∏O_i (O_i the rings of integers of the factors K_i of ℚ_ℓ[T]/(f)); with V = ⊕K_i^{n_i}, every full γ-stable ℤ_ℓ-lattice is ⊕(free O_i-lattices of rank n_i), the centralizer ∏GL_{n_i}(K_i) acts transitively on them, and the stabilizer of one is conjugate to ∏GL_{n_i}(O_i).
hypotheses: The discriminant is that of the squarefree minimal polynomial, not of the characteristic polynomial.
proofSteps: Unit discriminant: R is étale, hence normal, hence the maximal order ∏O_i (monogenic-order index ℓ^δ with δ = 0).
A γ-stable lattice is an R-module, hence decomposes along the idempotents of R, and each component is a finitely generated torsion-free module over the DVR O_i, hence free.
acceptance: γ = diag(1, 2) on ℚ_3²: f = (T − 1)(T − 2), disc = 1, the stable lattices are ℤ_3a ⊕ ℤ_3b, one orbit under the diagonal torus.

sources.match: Decomposes V_ℓ by the irreducible factors of the minimal polynomial and reduces orbit counting to the isotypic R-lattices; at primes where the discriminant is a unit the colength bound δ is 0, giving a single orbit.

nodes.title: Orders in finite-dimensional algebras and quaternion orders
nodes.statement: Let R be a noetherian domain with fraction field F and B a finite-dimensional F-algebra. An R-order in B is an R-lattice O ⊆ B (finitely generated, spanning B over F) that is a subring, so 1 ∈ O and R ⊆ O; it is maximal if it is not properly contained in another R-order. Every element of an order is integral over R. A quaternion order is an order in a quaternion algebra B = (a, b | F); it is stable under the standard involution x ↦ x̄ (as x̄ = trd(x) − x with trd(x) ∈ R), and the reduced norm and trace restrict to R-valued maps on it.
hypotheses: R noetherian domain; for quaternion orders R is a Dedekind domain with F of characteristic ≠ 2 where the standard involution is used.
This is the general notion that ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.7 (orders in finite-dimensional algebras, maximal orders) also uses; it is planned here and CA.7 imports it.
proofSteps: Integrality: an element of an order generates a finitely generated R-submodule, hence is integral (Voight Lemma 10.3.2).
Standard-involution stability: x ∈ O is integral, so its reduced characteristic polynomial x² − trd(x)x + nrd(x) has coefficients in R (R integrally closed), and x̄ = trd(x) − x ∈ O.
acceptance: M₂(ℤ) ⊆ M₂(ℚ) is a maximal order.
The Lipschitz order ℤ⟨i, j⟩ in (−1, −1 | ℚ) is an order, not maximal (contained in the Hurwitz order).

nodes.title: Discriminant and reduced discriminant of a quaternion order
nodes.statement: For an R-lattice I in a quaternion algebra B over F (R Dedekind), disc(I) is the R-submodule of F generated by d(α_1, …, α_4) = det(trd(α_iα_j)), and the reduced discriminant discrd(I) is generated by the values of the alternating trilinear form m(α_1, α_2, α_3) = trd((α_1α_2 − α_2α_1)α_3) on I. disc(I) = [J : I]²disc(J) for projective lattices; for R-orders O ⊆ O′, disc(O) = discrd(O)² and discrd(O) = [O′ : O]·discrd(O′) (both fail for lattices that are not orders: see source issue E201); for an order with a free basis disc(O) = d(basis)R. Discriminants localize and complete, and O ⊆ O′ with equal discriminants forces O = O′.
hypotheses: R Dedekind with fraction field F; B a quaternion algebra over F; lattices projective.
proofSteps: disc is the discriminant ideal of the reduced-trace pairing (lattice-discriminant-ideal) and inherits its index law (Voight Lemma 15.2.15).

m is alternating and well defined on B/F (Voight Lemma 15.4.3); m(α_1, α_2, α_3)² = −d(1, α_1, α_2, α_3), and for an order the values d(1, α_1, α_2, α_3) generate disc(O), giving disc = discrd² (Lemma 15.4.7, valid for orders: an order contains R·1 as a saturated summand, so its index in another order is the index of the images in B/F).
acceptance: discrd(M₂(ℤ)) = ℤ.
Hurwitz order: discrd = 2ℤ; Lipschitz order ℤ⟨i, j⟩: discrd = 4ℤ = [Hurwitz : Lipschitz]·2ℤ.

nodes.title: Maximal quaternion orders and the reduced discriminant
nodes.statement: Let R be a Dedekind domain whose fraction field F is a global field (a global ring), B a quaternion algebra over F and disc_R(B) the product of the primes of R at which B ramifies. Every R-order is contained in a maximal one, and an order O is maximal iff discrd(O) = disc_R(B). Locally: over a DVR, an order in M₂(F) is maximal iff its discriminant is R, and then it is conjugate to M₂(R); in a division quaternion algebra over a nonarchimedean local field the valuation ring is the unique maximal order, with discrd = 𝔭.
hypotheses: R Dedekind with global fraction field; B quaternion over F.
proofSteps: Existence: an ascending chain of orders has strictly increasing discriminants (quaternion-order-discriminant), which stabilizes since R is noetherian.
Local split case: maximal orders of M₂(F) over a DVR are conjugate to M₂(R) (Voight Corollary 10.5.5), whose discriminant is R; conversely an order of discriminant R is maximal by the index law.
Local division case: the valuation ring is the set of integral elements, hence the unique maximal order (Voight Proposition 13.3.4), with discrd 𝔭.
Global: maximality is local and discrd localizes; compare prime by prime.
acceptance: (−1, −1 | ℚ): Hurwitz order, discrd = 2 = disc B, maximal.
The Lipschitz order has discrd 4 ≠ 2, not maximal.

sources.locator: Proposition 13.3.4, printed p.199; Theorem 13.3.11, p.200; Lemma 15.5.1, Proposition 15.5.2, Lemma 15.5.3, Example 15.5.4, p.240; Theorem 15.5.5 and Example 15.5.7, p.241
sources.match: Proves the valuation ring of a local division algebra is the unique maximal order, the existence of maximal orders through discriminants, the local split criterion disc = R, and the global criterion discrd(O) = disc(B) with explicit maximal orders of prime discriminant.

nodes.title: Reduced norms from a quaternion algebra (Hasse–Schilling, Eichler)
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, B a quaternion algebra over F and Ω the set of real places at which B ramifies. Then nrd(B^×) = F^×_{>_Ω 0} = {x ∈ F^× : x_v > 0 for all v ∈ Ω}. Locally, nrd(B_v^×) = ℝ_{>0} if B_v ≅ ℍ and F_v^× otherwise, and nrd(O_v^×) = R_v^× for a maximal order O_v at a finite place.
hypotheses: F a number field; the statement at real places uses the sign at the ramified ones only.
proofSteps: nrd is the norm form of B (Tau Ceti QuaternionAlgebra.normForm), a 4-dimensional quadratic form; x ∈ B^× has nrd(x) = c iff the norm form represents c.

Local: if B_v is split the norm form is hyperbolic, hence universal; if B_v is a division algebra over a nonarchimedean field, ⟨−c⟩ ⊥ nrd is 5-dimensional and therefore isotropic, so nrd represents c; at a real ramified place nrd is positive definite (Voight Lemma 13.4.9).
Global: by the Hasse principle for representations of scalars (GlobalQuadraticForms Layer 6), c is represented globally iff it is represented at every place.
Units of a maximal order: nrd(O_v^×) = R_v^× from the explicit maximal orders (Voight Lemma 13.4.9).

If B is split, det diag(c,1)=c gives the norm directly. In the division case, isotropy of nrd(x)−cz² forces z≠0, so nrd(x/z)=c. This is the point at which division, rather than just regularity, is used.
acceptance: B = (−1, −1 | ℚ) (ramified at 2 and ∞): nrd(B^×) = ℚ_{>0}, and 3 = nrd(1 + i + j).
B = M₂(F): nrd = det is onto F^×.

nodes.title: Quadratic forms over a finite field
nodes.statement: Let F = 𝔽_q. (a) Every quadratic form of dimension ≥ 3 is isotropic, and every nondegenerate form of dimension ≥ 2 represents every element of F^×. (b) For q odd, nondegenerate quadratic forms are classified by dimension and discriminant in F^×/F^{×2} (two classes in each positive dimension). (c) For q even, nondegenerate (nonsingular) forms of even dimension 2m are classified by dimension and Arf invariant (arf-invariant): the hyperbolic form mH and the form (m−1)H ⊥ [1, c] with c ∉ ℘(F); in each odd dimension there is one regular odd-dimensional form up to isometry.
hypotheses: Nondegenerate in characteristic 2 means the polar form has radical of dimension ≤ 1 and q is anisotropic on it (EKM's convention).
proofSteps: (a) Chevalley–Warning (Mathlib char_dvd_card_solutions_of_sum_lt) gives a nontrivial zero in dimension ≥ 3; a nondegenerate binary form ⊥ ⟨−c⟩ (or [·,·] ⊥ ⟨c⟩) is isotropic, so the binary form represents c.

(b) Split off hyperbolic planes (Witt decomposition, QuadraticFormInvariants Layer 1) down to an anisotropic part of dimension ≤ 2; binary forms are classified by the discriminant (EKM Proposition 13.2), and F^×/F^{×2} has order 2.

(c) For a perfect field of characteristic two, a regular odd-dimensional form has a one-dimensional polar radical on which q is nonzero. Normalize that radical line to ⟨1⟩ since every element is a square. In rank at least three, Chevalley–Warning supplies a nonzero isotropic vector; it cannot lie in the radical. Pair it with a vector having polar pairing 1, then add a multiple of the isotropic vector to make that partner isotropic. Split off a hyperbolic plane and induct to get H^m⊥⟨1⟩. Even-dimensional forms instead have perfect alternating polarization; split hyperbolic planes to the binary remainder, classified by F/℘(F) and the Arf invariant.

For regularity in characteristic two, a radical line with q zero is excluded. The perfect-polar Witt decomposition imported from QuadraticFormInvariants is used only in characteristic ≠2; the characteristic-two splitting argument is supplied here.
acceptance: q odd, n = 2: x² + y² is hyperbolic iff −1 is a square iff q ≡ 1 mod 4.
q = 2, n = 2: xy (Arf 0) and x² + xy + y² (Arf 1) are the two nonsingular binary forms.

nodes.title: The Arf invariant
nodes.statement: Let F be a field of characteristic 2 and q a nonsingular quadratic form of dimension 2m on V, with a symplectic basis e_1, f_1, …, e_m, f_m of its (alternating, nondegenerate) polar form b. The Arf invariant is Arf(q) = Σ_i q(e_i)q(f_i) mod ℘(F), where ℘(x) = x² + x; it is independent of the symplectic basis, additive on orthogonal sums, zero on hyperbolic forms, and is the class of the discriminant algebra (the centre of the even Clifford algebra) in Ét₂(F) ≅ F/℘(F). Over 𝔽_{2^k}, F/℘(F) ≅ ℤ/2.
hypotheses: char F = 2; q nonsingular of even dimension (polar form nondegenerate).
proofSteps: Independence: the centre of C₀(q) is the étale algebra F[x]/(x² + x + Arf(q)), an invariant of q (EKM §13); so Arf is well defined.
Additivity follows from C₀ of an orthogonal sum; Arf(H) = 0 since q(e)q(f) = 0.
acceptance: Arf(xy) = 0.
Over 𝔽_2, Arf(x² + xy + y²) = 1.

nodes.title: Quadric surfaces over a finite field
nodes.statement: Over 𝔽_q there are exactly three PGL₄(𝔽_q)-orbits of geometrically irreducible quadric surfaces in ℙ³: the cone Q^con ≅ ℙ(1, 1, 2) (rank 3), the nonsplit smooth quadric Q^nsp (rank 4, isomorphic to ℙ¹ × ℙ¹ over 𝔽_{q²} with Frobenius swapping the rulings, Picard rank 1) and the split quadric Q^spl ≅ ℙ¹ × ℙ¹. Their automorphism groups have orders #Aut(Q^con) = q⁷ − q⁶ − q⁵ + q⁴ = #GL₂(𝔽_q)·q³, #Aut(Q^nsp) = 2(q⁶ − q²) = 2#PGL₂(𝔽_{q²}) and #Aut(Q^spl) = 2(q³ − q)² = 2#PGL₂(𝔽_q)².
hypotheses: The quadric is geometrically irreducible and reduced: geometric quadratic rank 3 or 4. A nonsplit rank-two binary norm equation is irreducible over 𝔽_q but splits into conjugate planes over 𝔽_{q²}; it is excluded. In characteristic two, quadratic rank here is not the rank of the polar bilinear form.
proofSteps: Finite-field classification, including the regular odd-rank characteristic-two argument, gives the cone q=xz+y² and the two smooth rank-four classes up to scaling. The split class is ℙ¹×ℙ¹; the nonsplit class is its twist with exchanged rulings.

For smooth quadrics, the complete hyperplane series identifies geometric automorphisms with (PGL₂×PGL₂)⋊C₂; Frobenius-fixed points give the stated split and nonsplit orders. For the cone, use its weighted model ℙ(1,1,2). The map to PGL₂ on the ruling has kernel z↦αz+f₂(x,y), of order (q−1)q³; multiplying by #PGL₂(𝔽_q)=q(q²−1) yields q⁷−q⁶−q⁵+q⁴. Only this order and exact kernel description are asserted; an isomorphism GL₂⋉𝔽_q³ is not needed.
acceptance: For a nonsquare d over odd 𝔽_q, x²−dy² in ℙ³ is irreducible over 𝔽_q but geometrically reducible of rank two, and is not one of the three surfaces. This separates irreducibility from geometric irreducibility.

nodes.title: Odd unimodular lattices represent units primitively
nodes.statement: Let R be a henselian DVR (in particular, a complete DVR) with finite residue field k of odd characteristic and let M be a regular unimodular quadratic R-lattice of rank at least two. Every t∈R^× is represented by a primitive v∈M. In rank one, with generator e of norm u∈R^×, a unit t is represented primitively exactly when t/u is a square in R^×, equivalently a square in k^×. The ℤ_p specialization is imported from IntegralLattices 3C; this node supplies the general henselian-DVR version.
hypotheses: R a henselian DVR (complete DVRs are included) with finite residue field of odd characteristic, L a regular unimodular quadratic R-lattice. The ℤ_p specialization is imported from IntegralLattices 3C, rather than owned again.
proofSteps: The reduction M/𝔪M is a nondegenerate quadratic space over the residue field of dimension ≥ 2, so it represents t̄ by a nonzero vector (finite-field-quadratic-classification (a)).

A nonzero representing vector has a nonzero partial derivative (the polar form is nondegenerate), so Hensel's lemma lifts the representation to a primitive v ∈ M (Mathlib hensels_lemma for ℤ_ℓ; HenselianLocalRing in general).
Rank 1: Q(ae) = a²u.
acceptance: M = ℤ_3² with x² + y²: represents 2 = 1 + 1 and the nonsquare unit 2 primitively.
Rank 1: ⟨1⟩ over ℤ_3 does not represent 2.

sources.locator: §3.5, proof of Lemma 3.5.2, pp.15–16 (arXiv:1107.1221); the henselian-DVR statement is derived by the same residue-field/Hensel proof.
sources.match: Proves that a unimodular quadratic lattice over ℤ_ℓ of rank at least two whose reduction represents a unit admits a vector of that norm, by Hensel.

nodes.title: Eigenspaces of an isometry and the Cayley discriminant
nodes.statement: Let (V, b) be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear space over a field k of characteristic ≠ 2 and φ ∈ O(V) with characteristic polynomial g. (a) For eigenvalues λ, μ of φ with λμ ≠ 1 the (generalized) eigenspaces are orthogonal; V_λ and V_{λ^{−1}} pair perfectly, so for λ ≠ ±1 the sum V_λ ⊕ V_{λ^{−1}} is hyperbolic with discriminant (−1)^r, r = dim V_λ. (b) V = V_{+} ⊥ V_{−} ⊥ V′ orthogonally, where V_± = ker(φ ∓ 1)^N and V′ is the part where φ has no eigenvalue ±1. (c) (Cayley discriminant) If g(1)g(−1) ≠ 0, then dim V is even and det b ≡ g(1)g(−1) mod k^{×2}. (d) If φ is diagonalizable over k, then W = ker(φ² − 1) is nondegenerate, n = dim V − dim W is even and disc W = (−1)^{n/2}disc V.
hypotheses: char k ≠ 2; in (a) and (d) eigenvalues in k; (c) needs no splitting.
proofSteps: b(φx, φy) = b(x, y) gives b(V_λ, V_μ) = 0 unless λμ = 1, by applying (φ − λ)^N adjointness.

(c) Since 1 + φ is invertible, the Cayley transform ψ = (1 − φ)(1 + φ)^{−1} is skew-adjoint for b, so (x, y) ↦ b(x, ψy) is alternating and nondegenerate, with Gram determinant det(b)·det(ψ) a square (Pfaffian); this gives dim V even and det b ≡ det(1 − φ)det(1 + φ) = g(1)g(−1) modulo squares (Chenevier–Taïbi Corollary 3.6, after Gross–McMullen Proposition A.3).
(d) from (a): the reciprocal pairs outside W are hyperbolic.
acceptance: φ = diag(2, 1/2) on the hyperbolic plane: g(1)g(−1) = (−1/2)(9/2) = −9/4 ≡ −1, the determinant of the polar Gram matrix [[0, 1], [1, 0]] modulo squares.
φ = −1 on ⟨1⟩: excluded from (c) since g(−1) = 0.

sources.locator: Corollary 3.6, p.30 (arXiv:1907.08783)
sources.match: States that for γ ∈ SO(V, q) without eigenvalues ±1 the discriminant of q is Q(1)Q(−1) modulo squares, also attributed to Gross–McMullen Proposition A.3.
Decomposes the space of a semisimple isometry into the ±1 part and reciprocal eigenspace pairs and computes the discriminant of the fixed part.

nodes.title: Zassenhaus’s formula for the spinor norm
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic ≠ 2, (V, q) nondegenerate and γ ∈ SO(V, q)(k) with characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^a(X + 1)^{2b}Q(X), Q(1)Q(−1) ≠ 0. Then the spinor norm of γ is sn(γ) = disc(q|_{ker(γ+1)^{2b}})·Q(−1) in k^×/k^{×2}.
hypotheses: Spinor norm of Tau Ceti/OrthogonalSpinGroups 1D (CliffordAlgebra.spinorNorm), with the reflection normalization θ(τ_v) = [q(v)].
proofSteps: Use the orthogonal primary decomposition V=V_+⊥V_-⊥V′. On V_+, γ is unipotent and a square in SO: in positive odd characteristic its finite odd-order unipotent group gives a square root, and in characteristic zero the finite binomial polynomial gives one. A square has trivial spinor norm. On V_-, write γ=(-1)u with u unipotent; its norm is therefore that of −1, the determinant class of q|V_- because this dimension is even.

On the summand V′ with 1+γ invertible, the Cayley/Clifford identity gives θ(γ)=det((1+γ)/2) modulo squares (Chenevier–Taïbi Theorem 3.5). Its dimension is even, so 2^dim V′ is a square and det(1+γ)=Q(−1). Multiplicativity yields the stated formula. This does not assume the eigenvalues split over k.
acceptance: γ = −1 on a 2-dimensional space: sn = disc(q).
γ = diag(2, 1/2) on the hyperbolic plane (a = b = 0, Q = (X − 2)(X − 1/2)): sn = Q(−1) = (−3)(−3/2) = 9/2 ≡ 2, matching θ(τ_{(1,1)}τ_{(1,2)}) = [2] of the base packet's spinor-reflection-product.

sources.locator: Section 3.2, Theorem 3.5 (Zassenhaus) and its proof, pp.29–30 (arXiv:1907.08783)
sources.match: States Zassenhaus’s formula for the spinor norm of a special orthogonal element in terms of the discriminant of its (−1)-part and Q(−1), and proves it by orthogonal decomposition and a Clifford-algebra computation.

nodes.title: Integral spinor norms of regular quadratic modules
nodes.statement: Let R be a local ring (or any ring with Pic R = 1) with 2 not necessarily invertible, and (V, q) a regular quadratic R-module of rank n ≥ 3: q nondegenerate (perfect polar pairing), or n odd with invertible half-discriminant. Then GSpin(V, q) → SO(V, q) is surjective on R-points with kernel R^×, the Clifford norm ν of a lift defines the spinor norm sn : SO(V, q)(R) → R^×/R^{×2}, and over a DVR R with fraction field K of characteristic ≠ 2 this is the restriction of the field spinor norm: θ(SO(V)(R)) ⊆ R^×K^{×2}/K^{×2}. In particular for a unimodular lattice L_v over the integers of a local field, also at dyadic places, the spinor norms of proper integral isometries are units modulo squares.
hypotheses: R local (Zariski-local triviality of G_m-torsors gives the lift); regularity as in Knus IV §3 ('semi-regular' in odd rank).

Rank n≥3 for the GSpin/SO statement in this node. The fraction-field comparison assumes char K≠2; residue characteristic two remains allowed. Regular odd rank means invertible half-discriminant, rather than perfect polarization.
proofSteps: The sequence 1 → G_m → GSpin → SO → 1 is exact as Zariski sheaves for regular (V, q) (Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Appendix C); H¹_Zar(R, G_m) = Pic R = 1 gives surjectivity on R-points.
ν(γ̃) ∈ R^× is well defined modulo squares since the kernel R^× has ν(t) = t².

Compatibility with the field spinor norm: a lift over R is a lift over K, and the field spinor norm is the Clifford norm of an even Lipschitz lift (OrthogonalSpinGroups 1D, spinorNorm_vectorRepresentation).
acceptance: R = ℤ_2, V = hyperbolic plane: diag(u, u^{−1}) for u ∈ ℤ_2^× has spinor norm [u], a unit class.
R = ℤ_2: the rational isometry diag(2, 1/2) of the hyperbolic plane does not preserve ℤ_2e ⊕ ℤ_2f, consistently with its spinor norm [2] not being a unit class.

sources.locator: Section 3.2, the definitions of non-degenerate and regular quadratic forms over rings, GSpin, Spin and the exact sequences (3.2.1), and the spinor norm over rings, pp.28–29 (arXiv:1907.08783)
sources.match: Introduces regular quadratic modules over a ring, GSpin with its Clifford norm and the spinor norm SO(V, q)(R) → R^×/R^{×2} when Pic R = 1, citing Conrad Appendix C and Knus.

sources.locator: Lemma C.2.8, pp.316–317; Clifford norm (C.4.2), p.337; Proposition C.4.6, p.340; (C.4.4), p.343; Corollary C.4.10, p.344.
sources.match: GSpin→SO is a smooth Zariski-locally split Gₘ quotient for regular quadratic modules; the Clifford norm on central scalars is their square. The Spin→SO kernel is μ₂ and its exactness is interpreted in the fppf topology. Pic R=0 turns the Gₘ torsor into a lift on R-points.

nodes.title: Characteristic polynomials of everywhere-integral isometries
nodes.statement: Let V be a free ℤ-module of rank n with a regular quadratic form q, G = SO(V, q), and P(X) = (X − 1)^a(X + 1)^{2b}Q(X) monic of degree n in ℚ[X] with Q(1)Q(−1) ≠ 0. If for every prime p there is γ_p ∈ G(ℤ_p) with characteristic polynomial P, then |Q(−1)| is a square when b = 0, and |Q(1)| is a square when a = 0.
hypotheses: q regular over ℤ (unimodular in even rank, half-discriminant ±1 in odd rank).
proofSteps: For b = 0, Zassenhaus gives sn(γ_p) = Q(−1) mod squares, and regular-quadratic-module-spinor-norm makes it a p-adic unit times a square at every p; so Q(−1) ∈ ℚ^× has even valuation at every prime, i.e. |Q(−1)| is a square.
For a = 0 apply the same to −γ_p (which lies in SO when n is even) with the roles of ±1 exchanged.
acceptance: n = 2, V the hyperbolic plane, P = X² − 3X + 1: Q(−1) = 5 is not a square, so P cannot occur at every p; indeed SO(V)(ℤ_p) = {diag(u, u^{−1})} and P has no root in ℤ_p for p inert in ℚ(√5).
Chenevier–Taïbi remark: for p ≡ 1 mod 4 there is no element of order p in SO_{p−1}(ℚ) since Φ_p(1)Φ_p(−1) = p is not a square.

sources.locator: Proposition 3.7 and its proof, p.30 (arXiv:1907.08783)
sources.match: Proves that if a regular form over ℤ admits local integral special orthogonal elements with characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^a(X + 1)^{2b}Q at every p, then |Q(−1)| (b = 0) or |Q(1)| (a = 0) is a square, by lifting to GSpin and Zassenhaus’s formula.

nodes.title: Local spinor images of unimodular stabilizers at all places
nodes.statement: Let K be a nonarchimedean local field with ring of integers R and L a unimodular quadratic R-lattice (regular in the sense of regular-quadratic-module-spinor-norm) of rank n ≥ 3 in V = KL. Then θ(SO(L)) ⊆ R^×K^{×2}/K^{×2}; if moreover K is nondyadic, or L contains a hyperbolic plane over R, equality holds. In particular the adelic spinor norm of an adelic proper isometry is a unit at almost all places (the base packet's spinor-adelic-norm) and the reference groups θ_v(SO(L_v)) are R_v^×K_v^{×2} at every place where L_v is regular of rank ≥ 3 and contains a hyperbolic plane.
hypotheses: The general dyadic image for non-split unimodular or non-unimodular lattices is not claimed (Beli's theory of integral spinor norms over dyadic fields); see the gap recorded for it.

K has characteristic ≠2. This node extends the reference-stabilizer result to finite extensions of ℚ_p; the ℚ_p/ℤ_p specialization and its proper spinor-genus machinery remain IntegralLattices 4C and OrthogonalSpinGroups 3C. Rank-two torus and rank-one adelic quotients are not asserted.
proofSteps: Inclusion for n≥3 follows from regular-quadratic-module-spinor-norm, including dyadic residue characteristic.

At odd residue characteristic, the complete-DVR unit-representation theorem gives vectors with arbitrary prescribed unit norms. Reflections in unit-norm vectors are integral; products of two reflections are proper and attain every unit square class. This extends the imported ℤ_p result without duplicating its ownership.

If L contains H=Re+Rf with q(xe+yf)=xy, reflections in e+f and e+uf are integral even when 2 is not a unit, because their norms are units. Their product is proper with spinor norm [u], proving equality in the dyadic split case.
acceptance: Rank 1 is excluded: SO(L) is trivial and θ = 1 ≠ R^×K^{×2}/K^{×2}.
